title: Logarithmic fully retroactive priority queues
formal: Does a deterministic fully retroactive priority queue exist with \(O(m+1)\) space and \(O(\log(2+m))\) amortized time per operation, where \(m\) is the number of operations in its represented history? It must support adding or removing a historical insertion or extract-min and asking for the minimum immediately after any supplied historical time.
definitions: The comparison pointer machine stores constant-size records with a fixed number of pointer and data fields, accessed through a constant number of pointer registers. A step can follow or change a pointer, allocate a record, compare two keys or perform a constant-size control operation. Keys are opaque members of a totally ordered set; pointer arithmetic, array indexing by computed integers and unit-cost unbounded counters are unavailable. All work, including rebuilding, is charged. A history consists of insertion records \((t,x)\) and extract-min records \(t\), with pairwise distinct timestamps in an opaque totally ordered time domain. Replay records by timestamp from an empty queue. Inserted items have distinct identities and ordered priorities; ties are resolved by identity. Histories supplied after each edit are promised valid: extract-min never acts on an empty queue. An edit adds a record at an unused time or removes a named existing record. A query at \(t\) returns the minimum surviving item after replay through \(t\), or an empty marker. Removing a past operation changes the interpretation of all subsequent records. There is no monotonicity promise on inserted or extracted priorities. Space includes every retained historical record and index. For each finite edit/query sequence, the sum of \(1+\log(2+m)\) over operations bounds total computation within one universal constant; initialization is constant.
why: This asks whether complete access to a changeable operation history can cost only as much asymptotically as an ordinary priority queue.

context_blocks.text: Demaine, Iacono and Langerman introduced the retroactive model, which edits the past rather than merely preserving snapshots.

The April 2026 revision reports \(O(\log^2m\log\log m)\) time and \(O(m\log m)\) space for the general case. It attains logarithmic time and linear space for monotonic priority queues, leaving the unrestricted target open.

Queries must return the minimum at any chosen time.
